    setup_tracing ¶

    setup_tracing(
    app: FastAPI,
    *,
    service_name: str,
    otlp_endpoint: str | None = None,
    sqlalchemy_engine: Engine | AsyncEngine | None = None,
    instrument_httpx: bool = True,
    sample_ratio: float = 1.0,
    resource_attributes: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    insecure: bool = True,
) -> TracerProvider

    Install OpenTelemetry tracing and auto-instrument the app.

    Call it at module level, right after the FastAPI instance is built (or inside the create_app factory) — never from the lifespan. Request spans come from wrapping the app's middleware stack, and Starlette builds that stack on the first ASGI event it receives, which is the lifespan startup itself. A call from inside the lifespan therefore finds the stack already built, and the OpenTelemetry FastAPI instrumentation never wraps it; this function detects that case and emits a :class:RuntimeWarning instead of failing silently. Since FastAPI 0.142, such an app is still traced, by FastAPI's own telemetry: a SERVER span under the instrumentation scope "fastapi" with fastapi.dependencies / fastapi.endpoint / fastapi.serialization children and the newer semantic-convention attributes (http.request.method, url.path) — not the spans this function attaches. When the instrumentation does wrap the app, FastAPI turns its own tracing off for it, so a request is never traced twice.

    The database engine of :class:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.connection.AsyncDatabaseManager only exists after connect(), which normally runs in the lifespan. Leave sqlalchemy_engine out here and call :func:instrument_sqlalchemy_engine from the lifespan once the engine is connected.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    app FastAPI

    The application to instrument for incoming requests.

    		 required
    service_name str

    Logical service name attached to every span (service.name resource attribute) — this is how the service shows up in Jaeger / Tempo / Honeycomb.

    		 required
    otlp_endpoint str | None

    OTLP/gRPC collector endpoint (e.g. "http://otel-collector:4317"). When None, a console span exporter is installed instead — handy for local debugging without a collector.

    		 None
    sqlalchemy_engine Engine | AsyncEngine | None

    When given, instrument this engine so every query becomes a span. Only useful for an engine that already exists at module level; for the AsyncDatabaseManager engine use :func:instrument_sqlalchemy_engine after connect(). Silently skipped if opentelemetry-instrumentation-sqlalchemy is absent.

    		 None
    instrument_httpx bool

    When True (default), instrument outbound httpx calls so they appear as child spans. Silently skipped if the httpx instrumentor is absent.

    		 True
    sample_ratio float

    Head-based sampling ratio in [0, 1]. 1.0 traces every request; 0.1 traces ~10%.

    		 1.0
    resource_attributes dict[str, str] | None

    Extra resource attributes merged onto every span (e.g. {"deployment.environment": "prod"}).

    		 None
    insecure bool

    Whether the OTLP gRPC channel is plaintext. Defaults to True (typical for an in-cluster collector). Ignored when otlp_endpoint is None.

    		 True

    Returns:

    Name Type Description
    TracerProvider TracerProvider

    The installed (or already-installed) global
    TracerProvider

    tracer provider, so callers can register custom span
    TracerProvider

    processors.

    Raises:

    Type Description
    ImportError

    If the [otel] extra is not installed.
    ValueError

    If sample_ratio is outside [0, 1].

    Warns:

    Type Description
    RuntimeWarning

    When app has already built its middleware stack (the call came from the lifespan or after the first request), so the instrumentation is not attached and requests are traced by FastAPI's own telemetry instead.
    Notes

    When a TracerProvider is already installed — setup_tracing ran twice, or the host wired its own — it is reused rather than replaced: the FastAPI instrumentation is attached to this app and sqlalchemy_engine, when given, is instrumented; the httpx instrumentation is left as the first call set it.

    instrument_sqlalchemy_engine ¶

    instrument_sqlalchemy_engine(engine: Engine | AsyncEngine) -> None

    Instrument a SQLAlchemy engine created after setup_tracing.

    The engine of :class:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.db.connection.AsyncDatabaseManager only exists once connect() ran, usually inside the lifespan, while setup_tracing has to run before the lifespan. Call this from the lifespan right after connect(); queries then become child spans of the request span, bound to the global tracer provider that setup_tracing installed.

    The SQLAlchemy instrumentor is a process-wide singleton, so this traces one engine per process: a second call (for another engine, or after setup_tracing(..., sqlalchemy_engine=...)) only logs Attempting to instrument while already instrumented, and the second engine's statements produce no span.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    engine Engine | AsyncEngine

    The engine to instrument. An AsyncEngine is unwrapped to its sync_engine, which is what the instrumentor hooks into.

    		 required

    Raises:

    Type Description
    ImportError

    If opentelemetry-instrumentation-sqlalchemy (shipped by the [otel] extra) is not installed. Unlike the best-effort path inside setup_tracing, an explicit call does not degrade silently.

    make_bearer_token_dependency ¶

    make_bearer_token_dependency(
    tokens: JWTUtils | Callable[[Request], JWTUtils],
    *,
    soft: bool = False,
    bearer_scheme: HTTPBearer | None = None,
    cookie_name: str | None = None,
    query_param: str | None = None,
    accepted_typ: Collection[str] = (ACCESS_TOKEN_TYPE,),
    strict: bool = False,
    legacy_claims: Collection[str] = (),
    error_message: str = MISSING_TOKEN_MESSAGE,
) -> Callable[..., Coroutine[Any, Any, dict[str, Any] | None]]

    Build a FastAPI dependency that decodes a JWT from header/cookie/query.

    Returns the decoded claims dict so the caller can wire its own get_current_user on top, combining the decoded subject with the project's session / repository conventions.

    Token lookup order, first hit wins:

    1. Authorization: Bearer <jwt> header.
    2. The cookie_name cookie, when set.
    3. The query_param query-string value, when set.

    The header/cookie seam is what lets the same dependency serve both bearer clients and the cookie delivery mode of :func:tempest_fastapi_sdk.make_auth_router.

    query_param exists for cookieless clients that cannot set an Authorization header — chiefly the browser EventSource used for SSE, whose constructor accepts neither headers nor a request body. Prefer a session cookie (withCredentials) whenever the client shares the API's origin; reach for the query string only when cross-origin or a raw EventSource leaves no other channel.

    .. warning:: A token in the query string leaks into access logs, the browser history and any Referer header. Only enable query_param with short-lived access tokens (never a refresh token), always over TLS, and scrub the value from your log format.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    tokens JWTUtils | Callable[[Request], JWTUtils]

    The JWT helper used to verify the token, or a factory called with each request that returns it — for a helper built after import, in create_app.

    		 required
    soft bool

    When True, return None on missing or invalid tokens instead of raising. Useful for endpoints that work both authenticated and anonymous.

    		 False
    bearer_scheme HTTPBearer | None

    Override the bearer scheme. Defaults to HTTPBearer(auto_error=False).

    		 None

    make_jwt_user_dependency ¶

    make_jwt_user_dependency(
    tokens: JWTUtils | Callable[[Request], JWTUtils],
    user_loader: Callable[..., Coroutine[Any, Any, Any]],
    *,
    soft: bool = False,
    bearer_scheme: HTTPBearer | None = None,
    cookie_name: str | None = None,
    query_param: str | None = None,
    accepted_typ: Collection[str] = (ACCESS_TOKEN_TYPE,),
    strict: bool = False,
    legacy_claims: Collection[str] = (),
    subject_claim: str = "sub",
    error_message: str = MISSING_TOKEN_MESSAGE,
    session_dependency: Callable[..., Any] | None = None,
) -> Callable[..., Coroutine[Any, Any, Any]]

    Build a FastAPI dependency that returns the authenticated user.

    The dependency:

    1. Reads the JWT from Authorization: Bearer (or, when cookie_name is set, falls back to that cookie).
    2. Decodes / verifies the JWT with tokens.
    3. Pulls the user identifier from the configured subject_claim.
    4. Awaits user_loader(<id>) and returns the user it yields.

    user_loader is the single seam where the service maps payload[subject_claim] to an actual user. Returning None from it refuses the request: with soft=False that is an :class:UnauthorizedException, the same answer an absent subject gets. In soft mode it stays None, which is what the flag is for.

    Session sharing. When session_dependency is given, the returned dependency declares it as a sub-dependency and calls the two-argument user_loader(subject, session) with the request-scoped session. Because FastAPI caches a sub-dependency by its callable within a single request, the authenticated user is loaded on the same session the request's repositories use — so the instance stays attached and can be mutated / refreshed without the InvalidRequestError: Instance is not persistent within this Session that a per-loader private session would cause. Pass the exact callable your repositories depend on (e.g. db.session_dependency); a different wrapper would resolve to a second, distinct session and defeat the sharing.

    When session_dependency is None the loader is called with a single argument (user_loader(subject)) and owns its own session lifecycle — useful outside a request scope, but it yields a detached instance.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    tokens JWTUtils | Callable[[Request], JWTUtils]

    The JWT helper used to verify the token, or a factory called with each request that returns it — for a helper built after import, in create_app.

    		 required
    user_loader Callable[..., Coroutine[Any, Any, Any]]

    Async callable that receives the subject (typically the user id as a string) and returns the loaded user. When session_dependency is set it is called as user_loader(subject, session). Returning None refuses the request when soft is False (401) and yields None when it is True; that is the answer for a subject that resolves to no account. Raising :class:UnauthorizedException from inside the loader also works and lets you choose the message. Raising :class:NotFoundException reaches the client as 404 on a URL that exists, which a front end does not read as "session over" — return None instead.

    		 required
    soft bool

    When True, return None instead of raising on a missing or invalid token, and when the loader declines the subject.

    		 False
    bearer_scheme HTTPBearer | None

    query_param str | None

A service whose legacy tokens declared their type under a claim of their own (type, token_type) has neither typ nor an SDK fallback marker on any of them, so under the default every one of those refresh tokens authorizes any route for the length of its TTL. Such a service wants strict=True plus legacy_claims, and until v0.274.0 could only get there by not using this factory.

    make_token_dependency ¶

    make_token_dependency(
    secret: str,
    *,
    header_name: str = "X-Token",
    error_message: str = "Invalid or missing token",
    allow_unauthenticated: bool = False,
) -> Callable[..., Coroutine[Any, Any, None]]

    Build a FastAPI dependency that validates a shared-secret header.

    The returned coroutine compares the inbound header value with secret using :func:hmac.compare_digest (constant-time).

    An empty (or whitespace-only) secret raises :class:ValueError here, when the dependency is built — at import, in a typical service. It used to disable the check silently, and a TOKEN_SECRET left empty in a deployed .env turned every gated route into a public one. A local run that wants the gate off says so with allow_unauthenticated=True; with a non-empty secret that flag changes nothing.

    While the check is enforced, every response of a route behind it carries Cache-Control: no-store. A response cache in front of the app (the SDK's ResponseCacheMiddleware or a proxy) answers before the route's dependencies run, so a stored copy of a gated response would be served without the token ever being checked; no-store keeps the response out of every such cache, whatever header header_name names.

    secret str

    The shared secret to compare against.

    describe_validation_envelope ¶

    describe_validation_envelope(app: FastAPI) -> None

    Rewrite the 422 schema to the envelope the handler answers with.

    FastAPI documents the 422 it generates itself as HTTPValidationError with detail as an array, and every route with a body or a parameter references that one component. Registering :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.make_validation_exception_handler changes the runtime shape to the SDK envelope, so leaving the schema alone would ship the documented-versus-real divergence this SDK exists to avoid — in the one response a generated client is most likely to model.

    Rewriting the single shared component is enough: each route's 422 is a $ref to it. The ValidationError item loses input, which the handler deliberately never emits.

    Called by :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.register_exception_handlers when envelope_validation_errors=True. Wraps app.openapi so the patch survives the schema being regenerated, and is idempotent.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    app FastAPI

    The application whose schema to rewrite.

    		 required

    make_validation_exception_handler ¶

    make_validation_exception_handler(
    *,
    log_level: int = INFO,
    catalog: MessageCatalog | None = None,
    default_locale: str = DEFAULT_LOCALE,
    logger: Logger | None = None,
) -> ValidationExceptionHandler

    Build the handler for FastAPI's RequestValidationError.

    The 422 is the error a client sees most often and was the only one outside the SDK's envelope: FastAPI intercepts RequestValidationError in its own default handler, so it answered with pydantic's raw list and no code, and never passed through the :class:MessageCatalog a service configured.

    Two things this handler changes, both measured:

    • The envelope. The response is {"detail", "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "details": {"errors": [...]}}, so a client parses one shape for every failure instead of two.
    • The messages. Each entry's message comes from the catalog, keyed by the pydantic error type rather than by field, so a new field on a schema is translated the day it is added. A type the catalog does not carry keeps pydantic's own msg, which is already the English sentence — so English needs no table and cannot drift from upstream.

    It also stops echoing the submitted value. FastAPI's default 422 includes input for every failing field: measured, a password field that fails min_length puts the password in the response body, and SecretStr does not prevent it, because validation runs before the secret wrapper is built. details carries loc and type and never input.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    log_level int

    Level for the log line. Defaults to :data:logging.INFO, since a 422 is normal client flow.

    		 INFO
    catalog MessageCatalog | None

    Catalog used to localize each entry. None keeps pydantic's own messages.

    		 None
    default_locale str

    Locale used when Accept-Language is absent or matches nothing in the catalog.

    		 DEFAULT_LOCALE
    logger Logger | None

    Where this handler logs. None uses the SDK's own logger.

    		 None

    ValidationExceptionHandler

    ResponseCacheMiddleware(
    app: ASGIApp,
    *,
    store: ResponseCacheStore | None = None,
    ttl_seconds: int = 60,
    max_age: int | None = None,
    cache_control: str | None = None,
    methods: tuple[str, ...] = ("GET", "HEAD"),
    cacheable_status: tuple[int, ...] = (200,),
    vary: tuple[str, ...] = (),
    exempt_paths: tuple[str, ...] = (),
    exempt_prefixes: tuple[str, ...] = (),
    cacheable: Callable[[Request], bool] | None = None,
    cache_credentialed: bool = False,
    credential_headers: tuple[str, ...] = DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_HEADERS,
)

    Bases: BaseHTTPMiddleware

    Add ETag / conditional-GET and optional server-side response caching.

    Example:

    >>> app.add_middleware(ResponseCacheMiddleware, ttl_seconds=30)
>>> app.add_middleware(
...     ResponseCacheMiddleware,
...     store=RedisResponseCacheStore(redis),
...     ttl_seconds=60,
...     vary=("Accept-Encoding",),
... )

    Configure the middleware.

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    app ASGIApp

    The wrapped application.

    		 required
    store ResponseCacheStore | None

    When set, full responses are cached server-side and served without re-running the handler. When None, only ETag / 304 handling is applied.

    		 None
    ttl_seconds int

    Server-cache TTL and the default max-age.

    		 60
    max_age int | None

    Cache-Control: max-age value; defaults to ttl_seconds.

    		 None
    cache_control str | None

    Explicit Cache-Control value; when set it overrides the max_age-derived one. The default is private, max-age=<max_age> — private because the middleware cannot know whether a given route's body is personalized, and a wrong public there means a shared proxy serves one user's response to another. Set it to "public, max-age=…" deliberately, on a router that only serves shared content.

    		 None
    methods tuple[str, ...]

    HTTP methods eligible for caching.

    		 ('GET', 'HEAD')
    cacheable_status tuple[int, ...]

    Status codes eligible for caching (default: only 200).

    		 (200,)
    vary tuple[str, ...]

    Request headers folded into the cache key and emitted as Vary.

    		 ()
    exempt_paths tuple[str, ...]

    Exact paths that bypass the middleware.

    		 ()
    exempt_prefixes tuple[str, ...]

    Path prefixes that bypass the middleware. ("/api/sse",) covers /api/sse/stream. Matching is textual, so it also covers /api/sse-legacy.

    		 ()
    cacheable Callable[[Request], bool] | None

    Optional predicate; when it returns False the request bypasses caching.

    		 None
    cache_credentialed bool

    Whether a request carrying any of credential_headers may use the shared store. False (default) makes such requests bypass it — their response belongs to one caller, and the key does not identify callers. True folds a digest of those headers into the key, so each set of credentials gets its own entry; only turn it on once you have checked that the cached routes do not embed a second identity (a tenant header, a path-independent session).

    		 False
    credential_headers tuple[str, ...]

    Request headers whose presence marks a request as credentialed. The default covers Authorization, Cookie, X-Token (the header of make_token_dependency) and X-API-Key. Add the header your own auth reads when it is none of those: a request authenticated through an unlisted header looks anonymous, and its response would be stored under the shared key and served to the next caller before the auth dependency runs.

    		 DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_HEADERS

    Raises:

    Type Description
    ValueError

    When ttl_seconds is not positive, or when credential_headers is empty.

    OAuthAudienceVerifier ¶

    Bases: Protocol

    The extra call the token-in-hand endpoint makes on a provider.

    Deliberately not part of :class:OAuthClient: the redirect flow exchanges a code this service asked for, so it already knows the token is its own and needs none of this. Only POST /auth/oauth/{provider}/token — where the token is handed to us by whoever is calling — has to ask who the token was minted for.

    Keeping it separate also means a client written against an older SDK still satisfies :class:OAuthClient; it just cannot be used with the token-in-hand route, which refuses with :class:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.exceptions.oauth.OAuthAudienceUnverifiableException instead of trusting it.

    is_log_dir_unset ¶

    is_log_dir_unset(log_dir: str | Path) -> bool

    Return whether log_dir is the empty string that disables files.

    configure_logging(log_dir="") (and LOG_DIR="") means "no file logging". Handed to :class:~pathlib.Path, the same empty string becomes ., the current working directory — so a reader would list whatever *.log sits there, and a clear would truncate it. Only a str can be empty this way; a Path was built deliberately.

    LogSource module-attribute ¶

    LogSource = Literal['all', 'debug', 'info', 'warning', 'error', 'critical', '500']

    Selectable log source for the /logs endpoint.

    "all" merges every per-level file (excluding 500.log to avoid duplicating error.log rows); the rest map to a single file.

    rotated_log_files ¶

    rotated_log_files(path: str | Path) -> list[Path]

    List the rotated backups of one log file, newest first.

    :func:~tempest_fastapi_sdk.configure_logging rotates either by size (info.log.1 is the newest backup, higher numbers are older) or by time (info.log.2026-10-20, info.log.2026-10-20_13 for hourly rotation; later dates are newer). Both shapes are listed, so a reader sees the same history whichever mode wrote it — and a directory that switched modes keeps showing the files the old mode left behind.

    Order is by modification time, newest first, which is correct across both naming schemes; files with the same modification time fall back to the scheme's own order (lower number first, later date first).

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    path str | Path

    The live log file (logs/info.log). It does not need to exist.

    		 required

    Returns:

    Type Description
    list[Path]

    list[Path]: The existing backups, newest first. Empty when the
    list[Path]

    directory or the backups do not exist.

    RSAWebhookSignatureVerifier ¶

    RSAWebhookSignatureVerifier(
    public_key_pem: str | bytes,
    *,
    algorithm: str = "sha256",
    header_name: str = "x-webhook-signature",
)

    Validate RSA-signed webhook payloads (OpenPix/Woovi-style).

    Some providers sign each webhook with their PRIVATE key and publish a well-known PUBLIC key; the receiver verifies the asymmetric signature over the raw body. This complements :class:WebhookSignatureVerifier (symmetric HMAC) for those gateways. Uses RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 over a configurable hash.

    Requires cryptography (ships with the [webpush] extra, or pip install cryptography); the import is deferred to first use.

    Validate HMAC-signed webhook payloads (Stripe/GitHub-style).

    Providers usually compute hmac(secret, body) with a fixed algorithm and ship the digest in a request header (hex or base64). This helper centralizes the verification using :func:hmac.compare_digest (constant time) and exposes a FastAPI dependency that reads the raw body without consuming it for the route handler.

    dependency ¶

    dependency(
    *,
    error_message: str = "Invalid webhook signature",
    timestamp_header: str | None = None,
    max_age_seconds: int = 300,
) -> Callable[..., Coroutine[Any, Any, bytes]]

    Build a FastAPI dependency that validates the inbound webhook.

    The returned coroutine reads the raw body, verifies the header signature, and returns the body bytes so the route handler can re-parse it without re-reading the stream.

    Replay. The signature covers the body and nothing else, so a captured request stays valid forever — anyone who can observe one delivery can resend it indefinitely. Pass timestamp_header= to additionally require a fresh unix-timestamp header and reject anything older than max_age_seconds, which bounds the window a captured delivery can be replayed in. It is opt-in because not every provider sends such a header, and turning it on unilaterally would reject their legitimate traffic. The SDK's own :class:WebhookSender sends X-Webhook-Timestamp.

    The timestamp is not covered by the signature

    Only the body is signed, so an attacker replaying a capture can also rewrite the timestamp to a current one. The check therefore bounds accidental and opportunistic replay, not an active attacker who reads and rewrites the request. Closing that needs the provider to sign timestamp.body — the shape Stripe uses; when yours does, verify it with verifier.verify(f"{ts}.".encode() + body, signature).

    Parameters:

    Name Type Description Default
    error_message str

    Message attached to the raised :class:UnauthorizedException when verification fails.

    		 'Invalid webhook signature'
    timestamp_header str | None

    Header carrying a unix timestamp (seconds). None (default) skips the freshness check.

    		 None
    max_age_seconds int

    How old a timestamped delivery may be. Ignored unless timestamp_header is set.

    		 300

    Returns:

    Type Description
    Callable[..., Coroutine[Any, Any, bytes]]

    Callable[..., Coroutine[Any, Any, bytes]]: An async
    Callable[..., Coroutine[Any, Any, bytes]]

    FastAPI dependency that yields the raw body on success
    Callable[..., Coroutine[Any, Any, bytes]]

    and raises :class:UnauthorizedException on mismatch.
